opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question. Right now a lot of agent development is basically prompt engineering at scale. People write these enormous system prompts, sometimes thousands of words, full of rules, edge cases, "always do this, never do that." They work up to a point, but they're brittle. You fix one failure mode and break two others, and nobody fully understands how all those instructions interact.

What reinforcement learning offers is a different paradigm. Instead of trying to *tell* the model everything it should do, you define what success looks like, a reward signal or a verifier, and let the model learn the behavior through trial and error. So rather than writing "when the user asks about X, first check Y, then call tool Z," you let the agent attempt the task many times, reward the trajectories that actually solve it, and the model internalizes the strategy. Often it finds approaches that are more robust than what a human would have spelled out, because it has seen the failure cases directly instead of a human anticipating them.

A few things make this especially powerful for agents. First, agents operate over long horizons with many tool calls, and it's really hard to specify good behavior for every intermediate step in natural language. RL lets you optimize for the end outcome. Second, the knowledge moves into the weights instead of the context window, so you're not burning tokens and attention on a giant prompt every call, which helps both cost and reliability. Third, it's a scalable feedback loop: as you collect more tasks and better verifiers, the agent keeps improving, whereas prompt engineering tends to plateau and become unmaintainable.

That said, I don't think prompts disappear. They're a great starting point and a good way to bootstrap behavior, and in practice you'll often combine them: start with a reasonable prompt, then use RL, or even automated prompt optimization, to refine it. The hard part, honestly, isn't the RL algorithm anymore. It's designing good environments and good reward functions. If your reward is gameable, the agent will find the loophole. So a lot of the craft shifts from writing prompts to writing evaluations and environments, and I think that's a healthier place for the craft to be, because evaluations are something you can actually measure and iterate on systematically.

r001.rationale: The response describes rewarding successful agent trajectories and using collected tasks and verifiers in a feedback loop to keep improving the agent.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot at Bespoke Labs. If you look at how agents get built today, a huge amount of the work is somebody sitting there writing these enormous system prompts. You've got the task description, then twenty edge cases, then "if the user says X, do Y," then a bunch of formatting rules, and it just keeps growing. Every time the agent fails in production, someone adds another paragraph. And that's fragile. The model is juggling all these instructions in context, they start to conflict with each other, and you end up with this brittle thing where fixing one behavior breaks another.

The way I think about RL here is that it lets you move a lot of that knowledge out of the prompt and into the weights. Instead of telling the model "here are the thirty rules for how to use this tool correctly," you let it actually try the task, you give it a reward signal based on whether it succeeded, and it learns those behaviors directly. The prompt can get shorter and more about the intent, and the model carries the procedural stuff.

And there are a couple of concrete ways that plays out. One is tool use and multi-step workflows, where the thing you care about is the final outcome, not any individual step, so you can define a reward on the outcome and let the model figure out the trajectory. Another is robustness. A model that's been trained with RL on a task tends to generalize to inputs the prompt author never anticipated, because it's not pattern matching on a rule, it's learned what good looks like.

Now, the honest caveat is that RL only works as well as your environment and your reward. If you can't verify success, you can't train on it, and a lot of the early wins have been in domains like code and math where verification is easy. The interesting frontier is building environments for messier agentic tasks, where you have to be more creative about what the signal is. I think the teams that get good at constructing those environments are going to be the ones that stop writing thousand-line prompts and start shipping agents that actually hold up.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent tries the task, receives a reward based on success, and learns those behaviors directly, describing feedback from agent performance into learning as an advantage over adding prompt rules.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning gives us a way to move from specifying every detail of how an agent should behave to specifying what a successful outcome looks like. With a complex prompt, you’re often encoding rules by hand: use this tool in this situation, check your answer, recover this way if something fails. As you encounter more cases, that prompt keeps growing.

With reinforcement learning, the agent can try different approaches and learn from feedback on the results. Potentially, it can discover strategies that we wouldn’t have thought to put in the prompt, especially for tasks that require a sequence of decisions.

The challenge is defining that feedback. Can you reliably tell whether the task was completed well? And does your reward capture what you actually care about? If it doesn’t, you can get behavior that scores well but isn’t useful. So I see prompts as a useful starting point, with reinforcement learning helping improve the behavior where we have good ways to measure success.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent can try different approaches and learn from feedback on the results, clearly describing its outputs feeding back into learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning gives us a way to move beyond trying to specify every aspect of an agent’s behavior in a prompt. Today, you might write a very long set of instructions: here’s how to approach the task, here’s when to use a tool, here’s what to do if something fails. But it’s hard to anticipate every situation the agent will encounter.

With reinforcement learning, if you can evaluate whether the agent accomplished the task, you can let it learn from trying different approaches. The prompt still defines the goal and the constraints, but the model can learn the strategy—when to gather more information, when to take an action, and when to reconsider.

The challenge is getting that feedback right. You want to reward actually solving the user’s problem, rather than some proxy that just looks like success. So I see prompting and reinforcement learning as complementary: we express what we want, and training helps the agent become better at figuring out how to achieve it.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent can try different approaches, have task accomplishment evaluated, and learn from those attempts, clearly describing feedback from agent behavior into learning.
